newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Steepeners eyed, Trade on side.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Steepeners eyed, Trade on side.

text.p: When U.S. credit market players return on Wednesday they will likely second guess curve-steepening trades booked after the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) held rates steady on Tuesday.
But traders will pay scant attention to a report on U.S. merchandise trade on Wednesday, market analysts said.
"Really, the event of the week is the FOMC," said Suzanne Rizzo, domestic economist at MFR Inc.
"The trade deficit has been all over the map in the last three, four or five months. It's hard to imagine any number that would be outside the recent range," she continued.

The Commerce Department releases March international trade data at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT on Wednesday. The deficit is forecast to have narrowed slightly to $10.3 billion from $10.42 billion in February, according to economists surveyed by Reuters.
The credit markets usually don't focus much on trade data, unless the dollar reacts strongly, Rizzo said.
Meanwhile, bond experts said it was no surprise that the yield curve steepened in the wake of the Fed's decision to hold off on another interest rate hike.
The spread between yields of the two-year note and the 30-year bond widened about five basis points, to 70 basis points late Tuesday.

But with the market already starting to worry about the possibility of a hike after the two-day Fed meeting starting July 1, lower yields on short-dated coupons may look less appetizing on Wednesday, experts said.

The Street is anticipating the Treasury's auction of two-year and five-year notes expected next week. The question is whether a two-year yield of 6.25 percent is rich enough to clear the new supply, said Josh Stiles, a bond analyst at I.D.E.A. Inc.
The two-year was yielding 6.20 percent late Tuesday.

"I think where the market is going to be focused (Wednesday) is: do the people who as a knee-jerk reaction put on steepeners really have somthing going, or are they going to regret it when the two-year comes next week and the market is looking ahead to a July tightening?," Stiles said.
But with the Fed out of the way for now, the ball goes back into the court of the various releases of economic data, with next week presenting a fairly full schedule, economists said.

"There is not much on the calendar for the next three days. It could be that, on balance for the week, we move mostly sideways, with probably a small upward bias," said Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc.

"I would keep an eye on Thursday's (weekly jobless) claims. They can cause some noticeable reaction, depending on what happens there, given the fact that we had a very sharp (31,000) decline last week," Karydakis added.
